hcv_title: Wave Motion and Waves on a String
notes: 12 Objective I items rebuilt. One source item refers to a figure of two pulses meeting; re-cast as a verbal superposition question.

practice_bank.title: Practice — Wave Motion and Waves on a String
practice_bank.intro: Twelve questions on travelling and standing waves. A recurring theme: the medium sets the speed, the source sets the frequency.

sections.title: Describing a Travelling Wave
sections.blurb: Reading amplitude, direction and phase straight off the equation.

items.prompt: A sine wave travels through a medium. The minimum distance between two particles that always have the **same speed** is
items.explanation: Particles half a wavelength apart move in exactly opposite directions but with equal speeds at every instant, since their velocities differ only in sign. Particles a full wavelength apart also match, but that is a larger distance. Note the question asks for equal *speed*, not equal velocity — which is why $ \lambda/2 $ qualifies.

items.prompt: At a certain instant a particle in a sine wave has zero displacement. The nearest particle also having zero displacement at that instant is at a distance
items.explanation: A sine curve crosses zero twice per cycle, at points separated by half a wavelength. So the nearest other zero is $ \lambda/2 $ away — though that particle is moving the opposite way. A full wavelength away the particle matches in both displacement and velocity, but it is not the nearest.

items.prompt: Which equation represents a wave travelling along the Y-axis?
items.explanation: The direction of travel is set by the coordinate paired with time inside the bracket. Here $ (ky - \omega t) $ means the disturbance moves along $ y $, and the displacement $ x $ is perpendicular to it — a transverse wave along the Y-axis. The last two options contain $ y $ but are standing waves, not travelling ones.

items.prompt: The equation $ y = A\sin^{2}(kx - \omega t) $ represents a wave with
items.explanation: Use $ \sin^{2}\theta = \frac{1 - \cos 2\theta}{2} $, giving $ y = \frac{A}{2} - \frac{A}{2}\cos 2(kx-\omega t) $. That is an oscillation of amplitude $ A/2 $ about a constant offset, at angular frequency $ 2\omega $ — so the frequency is $ 2\omega/2\pi = \omega/\pi $. Squaring a sinusoid always doubles its frequency.

items.prompt: Which of these is a mechanical wave?
items.explanation: A mechanical wave needs a material medium to carry it, because it propagates by displacing particles that pull on their neighbours. Sound qualifies; the other three are electromagnetic and travel perfectly well through vacuum. This is why space is silent but not dark.

items.prompt: A cork floating on a pond bobs up and down at frequency $ \nu $ as a wave passes. The frequency of the wave is
items.explanation: Every particle of the medium oscillates at exactly the wave's frequency — that is what frequency means for a wave. One complete bob of the cork corresponds to one full wavelength passing it. The frequency is set by the source and never changes as the wave travels.

sections.title: Speed of a Wave on a String
sections.blurb: Tension pulls it along; mass per unit length holds it back.

items.prompt: Strings A and B are of the same material and under the same tension, but A's radius is double B's. The wave speeds satisfy
items.explanation: Speed is $ v = \sqrt{T/\mu} $, and mass per unit length goes as the square of the radius, so A has four times B's $ \mu $. The speed therefore falls by $ \sqrt{4} = 2 $: $ v_A = v_B/2 $. A thicker string carries waves more slowly, which is why bass guitar strings are the heavy ones.

items.prompt: Wires A and B are geometrically identical and stretched by equal small amounts. Given $ Y_A > Y_B $ and $ \rho_A > \rho_B $, a transverse pulse takes time $ t_1 $ to cross A and $ t_2 $ to cross B. Then
options: $ t_1 < t_2 $, since A carries the greater tension
$ t_1 = t_2 $, since the wires are geometrically identical
the given information cannot decide between $ t_1 $ and $ t_2 $
$ t_1 > t_2 $, since A is the denser of the two wires
items.explanation: Equal strain means the tension is $ T = YA\varepsilon $, so A carries the greater tension (raising its speed) — but A is also denser (lowering it). With $ v = \sqrt{Y\varepsilon/\rho} $, the outcome depends on the ratio $ Y/\rho $ for each wire, and knowing only that both $ Y $ and $ \rho $ are larger for A does not fix which ratio wins.

items.prompt: A wave passes from a thin string into a thicker one joined to it. Comparing the wavelengths, $ \lambda' $ in the thick string and $ \lambda $ in the thin one,
items.explanation: The frequency is fixed by the source and cannot change at a boundary — the two strings must vibrate together. The thicker string has a larger $ \mu $ and so a smaller speed, and since $ \lambda = v/\nu $, the wavelength shrinks with it.

items.prompt: The waves $ y = a\sin(\omega t - kx) $ and $ y = a\cos(\omega t - kx) $ are superposed. The resultant amplitude is
items.explanation: The two differ in phase by $ \pi/2 $, so they combine like perpendicular vectors: $ \sqrt{a^{2}+a^{2}} = \sqrt{2}a $. Amplitudes add arithmetically only when the waves are exactly in phase, and cancel only when exactly out of phase.

items.prompt: The superposition principle applies to the net displacement of a particle carrying two waves. Stated for the particle's **velocity** and its **kinetic energy**, such a principle would be valid for
items.explanation: Velocity is the time derivative of displacement, and differentiation is linear, so velocities add just as displacements do. Kinetic energy goes as the *square* of velocity, and $ (v_1+v_2)^{2} \ne v_1^{2}+v_2^{2} $ — the cross term is exactly what produces interference. Energy is redistributed, never simply summed.

items.prompt: Two identical pulses of opposite sign travel towards each other along a string. At the instant they exactly overlap,
options: the string is straight and completely at rest
the pulses have destroyed one another
the string shows a pulse of double the height
the string is momentarily straight but its particles are moving
items.explanation: The displacements cancel everywhere, so the string looks flat — but the particle *velocities* add rather than cancel, so the energy is entirely kinetic at that instant. A moment later the pulses re-emerge unchanged and continue on their way. Waves pass through each other; they never annihilate.

worked_examples.label: Example 1 — Reading a wave equation
worked_examples.problem: A wave is described by $ y = 0.02\sin(300t - 5x) $ in SI units. Find its amplitude, frequency, wavelength, speed and direction of travel.
worked_examples.solution:
Compare with the standard form $ y = A\sin(\omega t - kx) $.

**Amplitude:** $ A = 0.02 $ m $ = 2 $ cm

**Angular frequency:** $ \omega = 300\ \text{rad s}^{-1} $, so

$ \nu = \frac{\omega}{2\pi} = \frac{300}{6.28} = 47.7 $ Hz

**Wave number:** $ k = 5\ \text{rad m}^{-1} $, so

$ \lambda = \frac{2\pi}{k} = \frac{6.28}{5} = 1.26 $ m

**Speed:**

$ v = \frac{\omega}{k} = \frac{300}{5} = 60\ \text{m s}^{-1} $

Or equivalently $ v = \nu\lambda = 47.7 \times 1.26 = 60\ \text{m s}^{-1} $ ✓

**Direction.** The signs of the $ t $ and $ x $ terms are opposite, so the wave travels in the $ +x $ direction. Same signs, as in $ \sin(300t + 5x) $, would mean travel in $ -x $.

**Shortcut worth remembering:** $ v = \omega/k $ gets you the speed directly, with no need to compute $ \nu $ and $ \lambda $ separately.

worked_examples.label: Example 2 — Speed of a wave on a stretched string
worked_examples.problem: A string of mass $ 20 $ g and length $ 2 $ m is stretched by a tension of $ 40 $ N. Find the speed of a transverse wave on it, and the time a pulse takes to travel its length.
worked_examples.solution:
**Mass per unit length:**

$ \mu = \frac{m}{l} = \frac{0.020}{2} = 0.01\ \text{kg m}^{-1} $

**Wave speed:**

$ v = \sqrt{\frac{T}{\mu}} = \sqrt{\frac{40}{0.01}} = \sqrt{4000} = 63.2\ \text{m s}^{-1} $

**Time to cross:**

$ t = \frac{l}{v} = \frac{2}{63.2} = 0.032 $ s

**What controls the speed.** Tension is the restoring agent — tighten the string and waves move faster. Mass per unit length is the inertia — a heavier string responds more sluggishly. Note the square root: to double the speed you must **quadruple** the tension.

**Watch out:** $ \mu $ must be the mass per unit length in kg m⁻¹, not the total mass. Using $ 0.020 $ instead of $ 0.01 $ here would inflate the speed by $ \sqrt{2} $.

worked_examples.label: Example 3 — Frequency stays, wavelength changes
worked_examples.problem: A wave of frequency $ 100 $ Hz travels along a string at $ 50\ \text{m s}^{-1} $ and passes into a heavier string where its speed drops to $ 30\ \text{m s}^{-1} $. Find the wavelength in each string.
worked_examples.solution:
**In the first string:**

$ \lambda_1 = \frac{v_1}{\nu} = \frac{50}{100} = 0.5 $ m

**In the second string.** The frequency is unchanged — the junction point is shared by both strings and must oscillate at one rate:

$ \lambda_2 = \frac{v_2}{\nu} = \frac{30}{100} = 0.3 $ m

**The rule that governs every boundary problem.** Frequency is fixed by the *source* and survives any change of medium. Speed is fixed by the *medium*. Wavelength is whatever $ v/\nu $ requires, so it is the quantity that adjusts.

**The same logic elsewhere.** Light entering glass slows down and its wavelength shortens, but its colour — its frequency — is unchanged. Sound entering water speeds up and its wavelength lengthens. One principle, many settings.

worked_examples.label: Example 4 — Standing waves on a string fixed at both ends
worked_examples.problem: A string of length $ 1.5 $ m fixed at both ends carries waves at $ 60\ \text{m s}^{-1} $. Find its fundamental frequency and the first two overtones.
worked_examples.solution:
Both ends are fixed, so both must be nodes. The longest wave that fits has one loop, of length $ \lambda/2 $.

**Fundamental:**

$ \frac{\lambda_1}{2} = L \Rightarrow \lambda_1 = 2L = 3 $ m

$ \nu_1 = \frac{v}{\lambda_1} = \frac{60}{3} = 20 $ Hz

**Harmonics.** In general $ \nu_n = \frac{nv}{2L} $, so

First overtone (2nd harmonic): $ \nu_2 = 40 $ Hz

Second overtone (3rd harmonic): $ \nu_3 = 60 $ Hz

**All integer multiples are allowed**, which is what gives a plucked string its musical quality — the ear hears the fundamental as the pitch and the harmonics as timbre.

**Watch the vocabulary.** The first *overtone* is the second *harmonic*. Overtones are counted after the fundamental; harmonics include it. Exam questions exploit this distinction routinely.

worked_examples.label: Example 5 — Tuning a string by changing tension
worked_examples.problem: A sonometer wire vibrates at $ 200 $ Hz under a tension of $ 50 $ N. What tension is needed to raise its fundamental to $ 300 $ Hz?
worked_examples.solution:
For a fixed length and string,

$ \nu = \frac{1}{2L}\sqrt{\frac{T}{\mu}} \Rightarrow \nu \propto \sqrt{T} $

**Take the ratio** so the constants disappear:

$ \frac{\nu_2}{\nu_1} = \sqrt{\frac{T_2}{T_1}} \Rightarrow \frac{300}{200} = \sqrt{\frac{T_2}{50}} $

$ 1.5^{2} = \frac{T_2}{50} \Rightarrow T_2 = 2.25 \times 50 = 112.5 $ N

**Note how steep the dependence is.** Raising the pitch by half again requires more than doubling the tension. Because $ \nu \propto \sqrt{T} $, tuning becomes progressively harder at higher pitches — and it is why over-tightening snaps strings.

**The instrument-maker's three levers.** Frequency can be raised by increasing tension, shortening the length, or using a lighter string. A guitar uses all three: tuning pegs for $ T $, frets for $ L $, and different gauges for $ \mu $.

worked_examples.label: Example 6 — Particle velocity versus wave velocity
worked_examples.problem: For the wave $ y = 0.05\sin(200t - 4x) $ m, find the maximum speed of a particle of the medium and compare it with the wave speed.
worked_examples.solution:
These are two entirely different speeds and confusing them is the classic error in this chapter.

**Wave speed** — how fast the disturbance travels along $ x $:

$ v_{wave} = \frac{\omega}{k} = \frac{200}{4} = 50\ \text{m s}^{-1} $

**Particle speed** — how fast a bit of the medium moves up and down. Differentiate $ y $ with respect to $ t $:

$ v_{particle} = \frac{\partial y}{\partial t} = 0.05(200)\cos(200t - 4x) $

$ v_{max} = A\omega = 0.05 \times 200 = 10\ \text{m s}^{-1} $

**The two are unrelated in direction and in size.** The wave moves horizontally at $ 50\ \text{m s}^{-1} $; the particles never travel anywhere at all, merely oscillating vertically at up to $ 10\ \text{m s}^{-1} $.

**The picture to hold.** A wave in a stadium crowd moves right around the ground, but no spectator leaves their seat. The wave transports energy and a pattern — never matter.

worked_examples.label: Example 7 — Power carried by a wave on a string
worked_examples.problem: A string of $ \mu = 0.02\ \text{kg m}^{-1} $ carries a wave of amplitude $ 1 $ cm and frequency $ 50 $ Hz at $ 40\ \text{m s}^{-1} $. Find the average power transmitted.
worked_examples.solution:
$ P = \frac{1}{2}\mu\omega^{2}A^{2}v $

**Angular frequency:**

$ \omega = 2\pi(50) = 314\ \text{rad s}^{-1} $

**Substitute:**

$ P = \frac{1}{2}(0.02)(314)^{2}(0.01)^{2}(40) $

$ = \frac{1}{2}(0.02)(98\,596)(10^{-4})(40) $

$ = \frac{1}{2}(0.02)(394.4) = 3.94\ \text{W} $

**The two squares are what matter.** Power goes as $ A^{2} $ *and* as $ \omega^{2} $. Doubling the amplitude quadruples the power; doubling the frequency does the same.

**Why this shape recurs everywhere.** Any wave's intensity goes as amplitude squared — sound, light, water waves alike. It is why the decibel scale is logarithmic, and why doubling a loudspeaker's cone movement demands four times the power.

worked_examples.label: Example 8 — Reflection at a fixed and a free end
worked_examples.problem: A pulse travels along a string towards its end. Describe what happens if that end is (a) rigidly clamped and (b) free to move on a frictionless ring, and state the phase change in each case.
worked_examples.solution:
**(a) Fixed (rigid) end.** The end cannot move, so its displacement must stay zero. The only way an incoming pulse and its reflection can always cancel there is for the reflected pulse to be **inverted**.

Phase change: $ \pi $ (half a cycle).

An upward pulse returns as a downward one, and the fixed end is a permanent node.

**(b) Free end.** Nothing restrains the end, so it overshoots to twice the pulse's amplitude. The reflected pulse comes back **upright**.

Phase change: zero.

The free end is an antinode.

**Why the fixed end inverts.** By Newton's third law the string pulls up on the clamp, so the clamp pulls down on the string, and that downward pull launches the inverted reflection.

**Where the same rule reappears.** Light reflecting off a denser medium suffers a $ \pi $ phase change; off a rarer medium, none. Sound in a closed pipe has a node at the closed end and an antinode at the open one. The physics of boundaries is remarkably portable.

worked_examples.label: Example 9 — Locating nodes in a standing wave
worked_examples.problem: A standing wave is described by $ y = 0.04\sin(5\pi x)\cos(200\pi t) $ in SI units. Find the distance between adjacent nodes and the frequency of oscillation.
worked_examples.solution:
In a standing wave the space part and the time part are separate factors — that is how you recognise one.

**Nodes** are where the string never moves, so $ \sin(5\pi x) = 0 $:

$ 5\pi x = n\pi \Rightarrow x = \frac{n}{5} $ metres, i.e. at $ 0,\ 0.2,\ 0.4,\ \ldots $

**Distance between adjacent nodes:** $ 0.2 $ m.

**Check against the wavelength.** $ k = 5\pi $, so $ \lambda = 2\pi/k = 0.4 $ m — and node spacing is $ \lambda/2 = 0.2 $ m ✓

**Frequency:**

$ \omega = 200\pi \Rightarrow \nu = \frac{200\pi}{2\pi} = 100 $ Hz

**Two facts worth carrying.** Adjacent nodes are $ \lambda/2 $ apart, and antinodes sit exactly midway between them, also $ \lambda/2 $ from each other. A node and its neighbouring antinode are $ \lambda/4 $ apart.

**How to spot a standing wave in an equation.** A travelling wave has $ x $ and $ t $ inside a single bracket; a standing wave has them in separate factors. Nothing propagates in the second case — the pattern simply pulses in place.

worked_examples.label: Example 10 — Two pulses meeting
worked_examples.problem: Two identical pulses, one upward and one downward, travel towards each other on a string. Describe the string at the instant of complete overlap, and account for the energy.
worked_examples.solution:
**At the instant of overlap the string is perfectly straight.** By superposition every displacement cancels: $ y_{net} = y_1 + y_2 = 0 $ everywhere.

**But the string is not at rest.** Particle velocities superpose too, and here they *add* rather than cancel — where one pulse is pushing a particle upward, the other is also pushing it upward, because a downward-moving trough lifts the string ahead of it just as a crest does behind.

**So where is the energy?** Entirely kinetic. A moment earlier it was partly potential (stored in the stretched, curved string) and partly kinetic; at the instant of flatness there is no curvature, so all of it is kinetic.

**And afterwards** the two pulses emerge completely unchanged and carry on in their original directions.

**The principle this illustrates.** Waves superpose; they do not collide. Two pulses can cancel in *displacement* at an instant without cancelling in energy — which is exactly why destructive interference never destroys energy, only relocates it.
